title: A certified sixteen-prime-factor lower bound for Lehmer's totient problem
journal_fit: The finite reductions, reproducible computational number theory, independently checked searches and primality certificates make a computational-number-theory journal the clearest fit.
contribution: The existing sixteen-factor lower bound and companion results are retained. A new self-contained appendix proves termination and completeness of a finite construction for every prescribed factor count k. It does not prove that all those outputs are empty; the full Lehmer conjecture remains open.
ai_scope: Claude through Claude Code assisted the original search programs, computational development, partial Lean work and drafting. OpenAI Codex assisted the ceiling and one-candidate reductions, targeted valuation and residue investigations, independent primality certificates, checking the stated finite reproductions, figures, editing and packaging. These efforts do not provide a full-conjecture proof. In this revision, Codex assisted the uniform factor-count construction, its proof, explicit-stack implementation, exact controls, title revision and submission files. The new appendix is supplied for author review and is not claimed as a full-conjecture proof.
formalization_scope: The repository contains partial Lean results for statements not depending on the exhaustive search. The full searches and the full Lehmer conjecture are not claimed to be Lean-formalised. The new uniform construction has a written proof and fresh exact controls; it is not Lean-formalized. The guarded k=14 run is explicitly incomplete.

abstract_tex: For a composite number $n$ whose totient divides $n-1$, earlier published work required fourteen prime factors, and computational announcements required fifteen. We prove a lower bound of sixteen, at least $16001$ if $(n-1)/\varphi(n)\ge3$, and more than $10^8$ if $3\mid n$, and that $n<2^{2^{k-7}}$ if $n$ has $k$ prime factors. For the companion equation $\varphi(n)\mid n+1$ we show that the nine known solutions are the only ones with at most eight prime factors, and that a further solution prime to $3$ has at least sixteen. Each statement is reduced by hand to a finite computation, which independent programs carry out. We also give a reduction with one candidate for the largest prime for each prefix and a uniform finite construction for every prescribed number of prime factors. The latter proves termination and completeness at each factor count; it does not prove emptiness for all counts. Lehmer's full conjecture remains open.
abstract_plain: For a composite number n whose totient divides n-1, earlier published work required fourteen prime factors, and computational announcements required fifteen. We prove a lower bound of sixteen, at least 16001 if (n-1)/phi(n)>=3, and more than 10^8 if 3 divides n, and that n<2^2^k-7 if n has k prime factors. For the companion equation phi(n) divides n+1 we show that the nine known solutions are the only ones with at most eight prime factors, and that a further solution prime to 3 has at least sixteen. Each statement is reduced by hand to a finite computation, which independent programs carry out. We also give a reduction with one candidate for the largest prime for each prefix and a uniform finite construction for every prescribed number of prime factors. The latter proves termination and completeness at each factor count; it does not prove emptiness for all counts. Lehmer's full conjecture remains open.
